steps.message: Reviewing the intake and the question.

claims.text: Goal entered: cut grid electricity by 30% by 2030 with a $400,000 capital budget in 2027. The baseline is the electricity the building buys from the grid after the solar already on the roof.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Efficiency only (Scenario A) does not reach the 30% goal: it cuts grid use by an estimated 6.2% to 17.6%.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Efficiency plus about 70 kW of new solar (Scenario B) reaches the goal at the low end, cutting an estimated 43% to 58% of grid use, and its cost fits inside the $400,000 budget.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: The full path (Scenario C: deeper efficiency, all free roof space and a backup battery) reaches the goal but costs far more than the budget, mostly because of the battery.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Rooftop solar alone on the free roof could offset about 57% to 63% of annual use. Efficiency is still part of the plan to keep the array small enough for the budget.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: P.S. 24 (X024), an elementary school at 660 West 236 Street, Bronx, built in 1953, with a flat roof of 40,500 sq ft (the user's number) and 135,600 sq ft of floor area. The utility is Con Edison.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Existing systems taken into account: the school already has 228.2 kW of rooftop solar. No existing efficiency work and no other renewables were reported, so the plan assumes none. Annual grid use of 226,605 kWh matches the city's 2024 energy report for this lot (Local Law 84), so it is treated as measured.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The city's building footprints show 40,497 sq ft of building outline on the lot across two buildings, close to the 40,500 sq ft roof typed in. A footprint is ground area, not a measured roof, so roof area still needs to be verified by an engineer or roofer.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The owning agency is the Department of Education (DOE). The city record shows no landmark flag. The record for this lot is listed under 660 West 235 Street, a different street than the 236 Street entered, which can be another frontage of the same lot.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The city's energy report shows the building also uses natural gas (about 4,353,100 kBtu, thousand BTU, in 2024), which is outside an electricity-use goal.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: A1: system losses of 18% (low) to 10% (high) around PVWatts' 14% default; weather is typical-year data.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: A2: usable roof setback factor of 0.55 (share of the roof assumed usable).
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: A3: array density of 66 sq ft per kW (kW is how much power at one moment).
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: A4: critical load not given, so estimated at 1.0 W per sq ft x 135,600 sq ft = 135.6 kW (a planning estimate, not metered). Backup length not given, so 8 hours assumed. Battery energy = kW x hours / 0.85 round-trip efficiency = 1,276 kWh.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: A7: efficiency measures (LED and controls) save 10-20% of annual use. This is a planning estimate, not a cited benchmark and not a building model.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: A9: prices are planning-level benchmarks, not quotes: solar $2,528-$3,752 per kW and battery $546-$812 per kWh (middle half of similar completed NYC projects, NYSERDA data), efficiency $1.17-$4.02 per kWh saved a year; standard efficiency saves 10-20% and deep efficiency 15-25% (planning estimates), and only 62%-88% of those savings is counted because the City's audited projects delivered that share.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: The baseline is 226,605 kWh a year bought from the grid, already reduced by the existing solar array. The city's report gives an energy use per square foot (EUI) of 48.4 kBtu per sq ft and an Energy Star score of 93, which suggests the building is already efficient and may leave less room for savings.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: A standard efficiency package (LED lighting and controls) is estimated to cut grid use by 6.2% to 17.6% and save $2,783 to $9,644 a year. The underlying 10-20% savings are planning estimates, not a building model. Lighting type was not entered, so LED may already be installed, which would lower these savings.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Only 62% to 88% of the predicted efficiency savings is counted, because the City's own audited projects delivered that share (Local Law 87 report); the trimmed percent is not added back.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Recommended: have an energy auditor confirm lighting, controls, cooling type and heating before buying efficiency measures; these answers were left blank in the intake.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Usable roof area is estimated at 22,275 sq ft (40,500 sq ft x 0.55).
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: A whole-roof array would be 337.5 kW DC, but the solar tool refused that size because the existing 228 kW array already takes most of the roof. This was a decision from the roof rules, not missing data: only about 109 kW of free roof is left, so the plan uses that size and never adds a second whole-roof array.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: A new 109 kW array on the free roof is estimated to produce 129,802 to 142,640 kWh a year (kWh is energy over time) in typical-year weather. The loss band is an assumption.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: That free-roof array alone would equal about 57% to 63% of annual use; the model credits no solar beyond what the building uses.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Roof area, free roof space, structure and shading must be verified by a structural engineer or roofer. Roof age and condition are not in the city's solar-readiness record, and the year the roof was last replaced was not entered.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Scenario A (efficiency only): reduces grid use 6.2% to 17.6% (21% to 59% of the goal); does not reach the goal. Typical upfront cost $39,769 to $136,643 (the median of similar NYC projects is about $87,016); net cost the same; simple payback 4.1 to 49.1 years; within budget; no backup power.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario B (efficiency plus solar within budget, 70.2 kW): reduces grid use 43% to 58% (143% to 193% of the goal); reaches the goal. Typical upfront cost $217,212 to $400,000 (median about $297,590); net cost $163,979 to $320,993 after a federal credit not confirmed for this school; simple payback 5.2 to 16.6 years (median 9.2); within budget (54% to 100% of it); no backup power.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario C (deep efficiency, 109.3 kW of solar and a 1,276 kWh battery): reduces grid use 66.6% to 84.9% (222% to 283% of the goal); reaches the goal. Typical upfront cost $1,022,406 to $1,619,785 (median about $1,317,361); net cost $730,504 to $1,185,923 after the same unconfirmed credit; simple payback 15.7 to 39.7 years; over budget; about 8.0 to 9.4 hours of backup for critical loads.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario C costs $622,406 to $1,219,785 more than your budget. Reaching the goal in this full-path form takes more than the $400,000 set aside; whether to extend the budget is your decision once the gap is compared with the savings.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Payback is a simple payback (cost divided by yearly savings), not a full solar-model analysis. Savings use the New York commercial average price of 19.81 to 24.18 cents per kWh, not this building's own tariff.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Yearly savings: Scenario A $2,783 to $9,644; Scenario B $19,296 to $31,793; Scenario C $29,889 to $46,545.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: The model treats the $400,000 as one total upfront capital figure.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Recommended Scenario B, line 1: standard efficiency package, typical range $39,769 to $136,643 (the median of similar NYC projects is about $87,016), based on 33,991 kWh saved a year at $1.17-$4.02 per kWh saved from completed NYC public-sector projects (NYSERDA data).
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Recommended Scenario B, line 2: 70.2 kW of rooftop solar, typical range $177,443 to $263,357 (median about $210,573), at $2,528-$3,752 per kW, the middle half of 239 completed NYC non-residential projects of 100-500 kW since 2022 (NYSERDA data).
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Recommended Scenario B, line 3: federal direct-pay credit worth 30% of solar, $53,233 to $79,007, counted in the model because the program page reports it open, with solar placed in service by 2027-12-31. Whether this school or its owner qualifies is not confirmed, so net cost ($163,979 to $320,993) may be higher; before any credit the cost is $217,212 to $400,000.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario C battery line: 1,276 kWh at $546-$812 per kWh (middle half of 56 completed or approved NYC storage projects, NYSERDA data), typical range $696,696 to $1,036,112, more than the whole budget on its own. Its efficiency line is $49,400 to $173,579 and its solar line $276,310 to $410,094.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Left out of net cost: the NY-Sun commercial solar incentive, because its current status could not be read from an official page (the dashboard blocks automated access). Check it in a browser before counting any incentive.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Left out of net cost: the NYC Solar Schools program (DCAS, NYPA and NYC Public Schools, rooftop solar under power purchase agreements). Its status is uncertain and it is not known whether this building is in the pipeline; ask DCAS or the SCA.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Local Laws 92 and 94 of 2019 are a rule, not an incentive: certain major roof renovations must include solar, a green roof, or both. If the roof needs replacing before solar, check this rule.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: None of the cost totals include replacing or repairing the roof. The roof's age and condition are unknown, and a roofer's quote is needed.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 0, confirm data and budget: gather 12 months of Con Edison bills, confirm the tariff, the 2027 capital budget and its type, and the real yearly output of the existing array.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 1, professional reviews: commission a structural analysis by a licensed PE or RA and a roof condition survey, including the free roof area beside the existing array. The roof cannot be certified from these records.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 2, efficiency measures: after an audit, install the standard package (lighting and controls not already in place) first, as the lowest-cost step.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 3, permits and interconnection: file the Con Edison interconnection application, hire a licensed electrician, and arrange FDNY rooftop access; route approvals through DCAS, NYC Public Schools or the SCA.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 4, solar installation: install about 70 kW on the free roof within budget, finished before the federal credit deadline of 2027-12-31 if the credit is pursued.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 5, battery, commissioning and verification: decide on the battery after the budget gap is compared with the value of backup power, then verify results against bills.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Scenarios A and B give no backup power; solar panels shut off during an outage without a battery.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Scenario C gives an estimated 8.0 to 9.4 hours of backup for the critical loads, emergency lighting and communications.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: A4: the battery size (1,276 kWh, 135.6 kW) rests on an estimated critical load and an assumed 8 hours, not metered data. Emergency lighting and communications alone may be much smaller than 135.6 kW, so a battery sized to a measured critical load could cost less; this needs a re-run once the load and hours are known.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: The current FEMA flood map shows zone X, an area of minimal flood hazard, so no flood-zone review is triggered. Only the flood zone was read; heat and winter-storm ratings were not looked up and the 2015 preliminary flood map was not checked.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Required: structural analysis by a licensed PE or RA, a roof condition survey, a licensed electrician, FDNY rooftop access review, and a Con Edison interconnection review. The roof cannot be certified from these records.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Because the school is owned by the Department of Education, approvals go through DCAS, NYC Public Schools or the SCA; the list at the end gives links.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Not triggered by the records: no landmark flag and flood zone X. Re-check if the 2015 preliminary flood map, which was not checked, changes the zone.
claims.label: FACT

claims.label: FACT

The system adds the link list at the end.

roadmap.footer_note: All figures are planning estimates with ranges, not quotes or guarantees. This plan cannot certify the roof; a licensed PE or RA must do the structural analysis.
roadmap.plain_answer: You asked how to cut the grid electricity at P.S. 24 by another 30% by 2030 on a $400,000 capital budget. The plan estimates this is reachable within budget: standard efficiency work plus about 70 kW of new solar would cut grid purchases by roughly 43% to 58%, for a typical range of $217,212 to $400,000 before any federal credit. Efficiency alone reaches only 6.2% to 17.6%. The school already has a 228 kW solar array, and the baseline of 226,605 kWh is what it buys from the grid after that array. The roof rules left room for only about 109 kW more, so a second whole-roof array was not an option. Adding an 8-hour backup battery pushes cost to $1,022,406 to $1,619,785, far over budget; whether to extend it is your decision. Roof age and condition are unknown. Next: confirm your bills and the existing array's output, then commission a structural engineer and roof survey.
